question: Can interpretable, quantitatively predictive hydrodynamic PDEs be learned directly from noisy microscopic active-particle trajectories or experimental video while respecting the system's conservation laws and broken symmetries?

key_findings.claim: Kernel coarse-graining followed by a Chebyshev-in-time and Fourier-in-space representation compresses particle data into differentiable hydrodynamic fields while retaining the slow collective modes.
key_findings.evidence: For the chiral-particle example, the authors coarse-grain 12,000 trajectories into density and polarization fields, filter a temporal spectral tail associated with fast fluctuations, and report that the resulting fields retain roughly one percent of the fine-grained spectral information. Exponential temporal spectral decay in all studied systems is used as evidence that deterministic rather than stochastic PDEs are adequate at the selected scale.

key_findings.claim: Physics-informed candidate libraries make conservation and symmetry constraints structural rather than post-hoc.
key_findings.evidence: Density-library terms are restricted to divergences so every selected model conserves mass. Coordinate transformation rules constrain tensor rank, while chirality is represented through the perpendicular polarization field; the final chiral polarization library contains 19 linearly independent terms and includes higher derivatives needed for length-scale selection.

key_findings.claim: Sparse regression recovers physically meaningful coefficients for the simulated chiral active-particle system and a minimal continuum model that reproduces its vortex dynamics.
key_findings.evidence: STLSQ with stability selection finds the continuity coefficient -0.99 versus the analytic -1.00, a chiral rotation coefficient 0.44 versus 0.50, and a density-gradient coefficient -0.60 versus -0.57. The sparsest stable polarization model has eight terms; coupled simulations produce long-lived vortices with comparable amplitudes, spatial spectra, time scales, density profiles, and vortex sizes to the particle system.

key_findings.claim: A model inferred from one short Quincke-roller video extrapolates to collective speeds, patterns, and boundary conditions not present in the fitting data.
key_findings.evidence: From about 580 frames spanning 1.4 seconds and roughly 2,200 rollers, the learned continuity coefficient is -0.95 and the advective coefficient is -0.67, close to theory and earlier experimental estimates. Simulations recover spontaneous transverse bands, predict roller speed as density varies, and form the experimentally observed vortex and reflected density shocks in square confinement.

key_findings.claim: The same pipeline also identifies an interpretable driven-flow model from fish-school video, but model selection still requires dynamical simulation and physical judgment.
key_findings.evidence: For about 1,024 sunbleak fish under a rotating stimulus, the method adds a perpendicular-velocity term, recovers the expected continuity equation, and selects the sparsest velocity PDE that spontaneously forms the observed anticlockwise vortex. Across all examples, regression produces a hierarchy; stability, pattern reproduction, and available analytic or experimental measurements determine the accepted model rather than regression residual alone.

method.core_idea: Translate discrete trajectories into smooth continuum fields, differentiate those fields spectrally, and use sparse regression over a library whose terms already obey known physics to identify compact hydrodynamic PDEs.
method.mechanism: Gaussian kernels produce density, polarization, or velocity fields. Chebyshev and Fourier transforms interpolate and denoise the fields and supply space-time derivatives. Candidate scalar and vector terms are generated from fields, gradients, conservation laws, tensor transformation rules, and explicitly broken symmetries. STLSQ is run along a threshold path with repeated half-sample stability selection, producing models of increasing complexity. Candidate PDEs are numerically simulated and compared with held-out dynamics, analytic coarse-graining, and independent experiments.
assumptions: A closed set of slowly varying hydrodynamic fields can be constructed from the observed microscopic variables.
The kernel width lies above microscopic interaction or mean-free-path scales but below emergent collective scales.
Filtered spectral derivatives are accurate enough that sparse term selection is not dominated by measurement noise.
Relevant operators occur in the hand-built finite library, and known conservation laws and symmetries are correctly specified.
The learning interval samples relaxation and other dynamically informative regimes rather than only a steady state.
Deterministic first-order-in-time PDEs are appropriate at the chosen coarse-graining scale, as inferred from rapid temporal spectral decay.

techniques.role: Maps particle positions and orientations or velocities to normalized continuous density and order-parameter fields.
Compresses, denoises, interpolates, and differentiates spatiotemporal fields while exposing fast-mode cutoffs.
Encodes mass conservation, tensor rank, chirality, broken Galilean invariance, and pattern-forming derivatives in the candidate search space.
Finds sparse PDE supports along a regularization path and estimates their recurrence across randomized half-samples.
Rejects sparse fits that are unstable or fail to reproduce collective dynamics and compares surviving parameters with physical knowledge.
Provides independent predictions for several coefficients and physical interpretations of learned linear and nonlinear terms.

evaluations.setting: 12,000 simulated heterogeneous chiral active Brownian particles on a periodic 100 by 100 domain
evaluations.metric: Recovered PDE support, coefficients, stability, and reproduced vortex statistics
evaluations.result: The continuity coefficient is -0.99 versus -1.00 analytically; two polarization coefficients are 0.44 versus 0.50 and -0.60 versus -0.57; the selected model reproduces long-lived vortices and their scales beyond the fitting interval
evaluations.baseline: Analytic kinetic coarse-graining and coarse-grained particle simulation

evaluations.setting: Experimental Quincke rollers from one approximately 1.4-second, 580-frame video
evaluations.metric: Coefficient agreement and prediction of flow patterns and density-dependent speed
evaluations.result: The method recovers continuity near -1, advection near the published -0.7 estimate, spontaneous bands, the speed-density relation, and confined-vortex shock patterns
evaluations.baseline: Earlier linearized Toner-Tu parameter estimates and separate confinement experiments

evaluations.setting: Experimental sunbleak fish under a rotating visual stimulus
evaluations.metric: Continuity recovery, selection stability, and spontaneous vortex direction and magnitude
evaluations.result: The selected model recovers continuity near -1 and forms an anticlockwise vortex; its support occurs in all reported subsamples at the selected threshold
evaluations.baseline: Coarse-grained fish trajectories and observed vortex

evaluations.setting: Spectral diagnostics for simulated particles, Quincke rollers, and fish
evaluations.metric: Temporal mode-power decay and robustness to filter cutoff
evaluations.result: Temporal spectra decay exponentially or faster and reported learned supports are robust over tested cutoffs

limitations: The operator library is manually specified; an omitted field, nonlocal interaction, multiplicative noise term, or high-order operator cannot be recovered.
Regression residual and stability selection do not by themselves choose the final PDE: the authors simulate candidates and use qualitative pattern agreement plus available physical estimates.
Kernel width, spectral truncation, learning window, and basis functions are consequential preprocessing choices that rely on domain knowledge.
The method assumes the selected coarse-grained dynamics are deterministic; systems with algebraically decaying temporal spectra would require a stochastic formulation not developed here.
Quincke and fish validations use limited videos and selected observables, with no broad multi-run out-of-sample uncertainty analysis.
Reported experimental coefficient uncertainties do not fully propagate tracking error, coarse-graining choices, library uncertainty, and boundary mismatch.
Code and datasets were available only on request in this version, limiting independent reproduction from the paper alone.
The demonstrations are two-dimensional; three-dimensional scalability is argued but not empirically tested.
failure_modes: Sampling only a steady state can make relaxation terms unidentifiable even when they control out-of-distribution behavior.
A slow process whose time constant approaches the recording duration can be thresholded out; the authors therefore fix rotational diffusion from single-particle measurements in one case.
Collinear library columns can yield unstable or nonunique supports despite sparse regression.
Too-fine coarse-graining preserves particle noise, while too-coarse smoothing erases the pattern-forming scales the PDE must explain.
A low-residual PDE may blow up or settle into the wrong attractor when integrated, requiring forward-simulation rejection.
Incorrectly imposed symmetry or conservation assumptions can structurally exclude the true dynamics.
Periodic fitting data can hide boundary terms needed when deploying the inferred model in confinement.
reusable_insights: Make hard physical constraints part of the candidate parameterization so every selected sparse model obeys them by construction.
Use spectral decay as a diagnostic for both the coarse-graining scale and whether a deterministic reduced model is defensible.
Collect training data during transients that excite candidate mechanisms, not merely after the system reaches its dominant attractor.
Separate equation proposal from dynamical validation: integrate every serious candidate and compare attractors, spectra, amplitudes, and extrapolations.
Treat independently measured single-particle coefficients as anchors when the video duration cannot identify slow modes.
Validate a learned continuum model under new densities, initial conditions, or boundaries rather than only reconstructing its fitting movie.
open_questions: Can weak-form or probabilistic equation discovery propagate tracking and derivative uncertainty into calibrated posterior probabilities over PDE supports?
How can missing hydrodynamic fields and nonlocal or stochastic operators be discovered rather than prespecified?
Can candidate selection be automated with held-out rollout scores and physical information criteria without visually choosing the first model that forms the expected pattern?
How stable are inferred coefficients across independent experimental runs, kernel widths, temporal windows, and laboratories?
What excitation or experimental-design policy most efficiently makes every plausible continuum term identifiable?
Does the approach remain tractable and statistically reliable for three-dimensional active suspensions and irregular moving boundaries?

competitive_landscape.title: Learning deterministic hydrodynamic equations from stochastic active particle dynamics
competitive_landscape.relationship: Also learns deterministic continuum equations directly from stochastic active-particle trajectories using physical priors and statistical model selection.
competitive_landscape.difference: It emphasizes stochastic-to-deterministic model reduction, learning latent phoretic fields, and statistical-learning guarantees; the reviewed work emphasizes kernel plus spectral differentiation, symmetry-built libraries, and experimental video extrapolation.

competitive_landscape.title: Data-driven discovery of active nematic hydrodynamics
competitive_landscape.relationship: Applies sparse PDE fitting to simulated and experimental active-nematic director and flow fields and estimates an activity parameter.
competitive_landscape.difference: It targets nematic orientation-flow coupling in microtubule experiments; the reviewed work develops a broader particle-to-field spectral pipeline and treats chiral polar particles, rollers, and fish.

competitive_landscape.title: Estimation of spatial and time scales of collective behaviors of active matters through learning hydrodynamic equations from particle dynamics
competitive_landscape.relationship: A later active-matter equation-learning framework likewise combines space-time coarse-graining, spectral representations, and sparse regression.
competitive_landscape.difference: It centers estimating characteristic scales in Vicsek and active-Brownian-particle simulations; the reviewed paper demonstrates quantitative coefficient and boundary-condition prediction from real experimental video.

competitive_landscape.title: Data-driven discovery of partial differential equations
competitive_landscape.relationship: Introduces the PDE-FIND sparse-regression paradigm that underlies operator-library equation discovery from spatiotemporal data.
competitive_landscape.difference: PDE-FIND primarily benchmarks continuum data from known PDEs; the reviewed work tackles microscopic particles and videos through coarse-graining, spectral filtering, active-matter symmetries, and dynamical validation.

competitive_landscape.title: Online Weak-form Sparse Identification of Partial Differential Equations
competitive_landscape.relationship: Uses weak-form sparse identification to reduce derivative sensitivity and update PDE estimates online.
competitive_landscape.difference: Its weak integral formulation is an alternative to the reviewed paper's global spectral differentiation and is designed for online data; it does not provide the same active-matter particle-to-hydrodynamics experimental workflow.

novelty_assessment: The distinctive contribution is the end-to-end combination of microscopic coarse-graining, global spectral denoising and differentiation, symmetry- and conservation-constrained sparse libraries, stability selection, and forward simulation on genuinely particle-resolved experimental active matter. Sparse PDE discovery and each individual ingredient predate it, but their integration produces interpretable coefficient estimates and nontrivial predictions across simulated chiral particles, Quincke rollers, and fish.
